summary: Discusses alternative ways of extending the Internet architecture to eliminate some or all unnecessary hops on shared media. It is informational and does not define a standard.

eli5.summary: If two houses are on the same street, mail should not go through a faraway post office. This explores ways to skip the extra stops.

questions: how to avoid extra router hops
subtitle: How to avoid unnecessary router hops when two systems are on the same network.

tldr.problem: When multiple IP networks share a common physical medium (like an Ethernet or switched public network), the Internet architecture could still require packets to travel through unnecessary router hops instead of directly between systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1620 explores four architectural approaches: hop-by-hop redirection (routers tell hosts about shortcuts), extended routing (routers know about same-medium destinations), extended proxy ARP (address resolution servers find paths), and routing query messages.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational and does not standardize a solution, leaving the choice to network designers. It established the problem formally and outlined trade-offs, influencing later protocols like IP over ATM.

today: RFC 1620 is informational and did not standardize a single solution. However, the problem it identified became increasingly real as switched Ethernet and ATM networks deployed. Later standards like RFC 1577 (Classical IP and ARP over ATM) addressed these issues for specific technologies. Modern network designs often separate shared media into multiple logical networks to avoid the problem, or use overlay protocols that abstract away the physical topology.

sections.title: The Problem with Shared Media
sections.content:
The original Internet architecture assumes that networks with different IP numbers are physically separate and can only communicate through routers. This worked well for traditional networks connected by point-to-point links. However, shared media networks violate this assumption: systems on a single physical medium can reach each other directly at the link layer without going through routers.

Examples include Ethernet LANs with multiple IP subnets, and Large Public Data Networks (LPDNs) like SMDS and B-ISDN, which can connect systems from different IP networks directly. The problem is that the standard Internet routing rules force packets between systems on the same shared medium to still travel through multiple router hops, wasting capacity and increasing latency.
sections.eli5: If two computers are plugged into the same Ethernet cable, they could talk directly. But the network rules might force their messages through two routers and back, even though there's a direct path.

sections.title: The Original Internet Model
sections.content:
The Catenet model, which underlies Internet architecture, uses routers to interconnect distinct networks. An IP address consists of a network number and a host number. When a host sends to a foreign address (different network number), it sends to a router. The router decides which router to send to next, based on its routing tables.

To actually forward packets across a hop, the sender needs the link-layer address of the target. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps IP addresses to link-layer addresses on broadcast media. Hosts also use ICMP Redirect messages to learn better paths. The RFC emphasizes that routing is centralized in routers, allowing hosts to be simple: they only ask whether a destination is local, and if not, send to their default router.
sections.eli5: The old model: routers are smart and handle all the routing decisions. Hosts are simple: send local traffic directly, everything else goes to the default router.

sections.title: Three Cases to Optimize
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three communication patterns that could benefit from hop elimination on a shared medium. First, host-to-host within the shared medium should be one hop. Second, host-to-exit-router should be one hop. Third, entry-router-to-exit-router for transit traffic should be one hop, since both routers see each other on the shared medium.

A fourth case, where a host outside the medium sends to a host inside, cannot be efficiently optimized without distributing per-host routing information, which would damage routing scalability. The RFC focuses on these three achievable cases.
sections.eli5: Three good opportunities: two hosts on the same wire should connect directly. A host should reach the router it needs directly. Two routers on the same wire should pass traffic directly.

sections.title: Four Proposed Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC examines four approaches, each with trade-offs. Hop-by-hop redirection uses extended ICMP Redirect messages (carrying link-layer addresses) to guide hosts to shorter paths. It requires only host and router changes, not routing protocol changes.

Extended routing modifies routing protocols to carry information about same-medium destinations and their link-layer addresses. Extended proxy ARP solves the problem at the link layer by having address resolution servers relay queries. Routing query messages introduce a new IP-layer mechanism for discovering paths.

Each approach has different implications for router processing, host changes, convergence after topology changes, and firewall interactions. The RFC does not recommend one but analyzes their relative strengths and weaknesses.
sections.eli5: Four ways to fix it: (1) routers tell hosts about better paths, (2) routers know about destinations on their medium, (3) address servers find paths at the link layer, (4) send a query to find the best route.

sections.title: Security and Firewall Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the extra router hops often serve a purpose: they allow routers to act as firewalls and security checkpoints. Direct shortcuts within a shared medium bypass these protections. Any solution must allow administrators to choose between optimization and firewall protection.

ICMP Redirect messages could be spoofed by a malicious host to divert traffic, though X(Extended)Redirects that carry link-layer addresses provide some validation. ARP remains inherently vulnerable to spoofing from anywhere on the shared medium. The RFC emphasizes that Internet security requires end-to-end cryptography, not just link-layer trust.
sections.eli5: Letting systems talk directly skips the routers that normally guard the network. We need to choose between being efficient and being secure.

sections.title: Architectural Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly rejects radical alternatives that would abandon the hierarchical network structure for shared media. Instead, it advocates evolutionary changes that preserve the core Internet architecture: routers interconnecting distinct networks, with hosts remaining simple.

The analysis established that shared media present a genuine architectural challenge and that multiple solutions are viable. The RFC leaves implementation choices to the community, noting that different scenarios (LANs, large public networks, ATM networks) might favor different approaches. This pragmatic stance influenced subsequent standards for IP over ATM and other shared-medium technologies.
sections.eli5: The Internet needs to grow to handle shared networks, but should not throw out its basic design where routers are in charge and hosts are simple.
